error_modes.label: Course deviation control on the inbound and outbound radial

texts.0: SP, due to course corrections applied without any reference to the rate at which the CDI was moving, did not stop the displacement from the selected radial after the intercept had been completed. The needle deflection continued to grow past 8 degrees from the course centerline with the aircraft still turning away from it. IP took the controls and re-established the aircraft on the published course.
texts.1: SP, due to a correction heading that only matched the drift instead of also closing the existing displacement, did not return the aircraft to the selected course once the deviation had developed. The displacement stabilized at the 8 degrees limit and stayed there until IP called for a larger correction. SP then turned toward the course, but the recovery followed the verbal prompt rather than SP's own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to a correction heading taken slightly too small for the crosswind component, did not hold the aircraft on the selected radial after the turn onto the inbound course. The deviation grew past 5 degrees and reached approximately 7 degrees before SP recognized the trend. SP increased the correction, regained the course and held it, with no intervention required.
texts.3: SP maintained the selected radial within 5 degrees throughout both the inbound and the outbound legs, keeping the CDI needle close to centered at all times. SP identified small displacements early and removed them with measured heading corrections. Course keeping stayed steady for the whole tracking exercise.
texts.4: SP held the selected course with a needle deflection that remained effectively centered for the entire exercise, inbound and outbound. Each drift tendency was detected at the first indication and cancelled with a heading change of only a few degrees. Course accuracy required no comment at any point.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft inside the course tolerance, but the CDI was held near the edge of the acceptable band for extended periods rather than centered, with a consistent displacement to the same side. Performance remained within standards, yet the pattern shows that the course is being contained rather than actively flown. SP is expected to work the needle back to center and to keep the displacement small enough that the tolerance is never the working reference.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the inbound and outbound radial with the IP flying the first corrections and talking through the CDI indications as each leg began. This is SP's first exposure to course tracking on this item, and reading the rate of needle movement rather than its displacement has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin reading the needle rate independently, with the IP available to confirm the picture.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the selected radial to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement reach the 8 degrees limit before the needle was worked back toward centre. The correction followed IP's call for a larger correction rather than SP's own reading of the CDI rate. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the correction from the rate of needle movement rather than waiting for the displacement to reach the limit.
texts_at.2: SP tracked both legs without prompting, letting the displacement grow past 5 degrees to about 7 degrees before the correction closed the CDI back to centre. The correction is still triggered once the displacement is clearly visible rather than at the first movement of the needle. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to correct at the first indication of needle movement so the working displacement stays smaller.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the selected radial within 5 degrees on three of the four legs, identifying small displacements early and removing them with measured corrections. The fourth leg needed a slightly larger correction after a momentary lapse in the cross-check, without affecting the standard met. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep the cross-check as consistent on that leg as on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the selected radial, holding the displacement to about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the needle was worked back toward centre. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP tracked both legs without prompting, letting the displacement grow to about 7 degrees before the correction closed the CDI back to centre. Correcting at the first needle movement, rather than once the displacement is clearly visible, would keep that margin smaller still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound course-tracking discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the selected radial within 5 degrees throughout both the inbound and the outbound legs, identifying small displacements early and removing them with measured heading corrections. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good instrument scan.
texts_above.4: SP held the selected course with a needle deflection that remained effectively centered for the entire exercise, detecting each drift tendency at the first indication and cancelling it with a heading change of only a few degrees. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding course-keeping precision.

error_modes.label: Wind drift assessment and correction angle while tracking

texts.0: SP, due to a wind correction angle that was never established after roll-out on course, did not compensate for the known crosswind and continued to fly the course heading as if in still air. The aircraft was carried steadily downwind and the deviation passed 8 degrees from the selected radial with no correction started. IP intervened to establish the required crab and to return the aircraft to the course.
texts.1: SP, due to a wind correction angle taken from the briefed forecast and never revised against the observed drift, did not prevent the aircraft from being displaced off the selected radial. The displacement built to the 8 degrees limit before any action was taken, and the correction followed only after IP pointed out the drift. SP then established a workable crab, but the response was late.
texts.2: SP, due to a crab angle removed too early once the needle started to return toward center, did not keep the aircraft steady on the selected course. The displacement re-opened past 5 degrees and reached approximately 6 to 7 degrees on the downwind side. SP re-applied the wind correction angle in good time and stabilized the aircraft on course without any assistance.
texts.3: SP established a wind correction angle appropriate to the observed drift shortly after rolling out on course and maintained the selected radial within 5 degrees. SP refined the crab in small increments as the drift was assessed against the needle movement. The correction held the aircraft on course on both the inbound and the outbound legs.
texts.4: SP determined the required wind correction angle almost immediately after roll-out and flew it precisely, so the CDI showed no perceptible drift for the remainder of the leg. SP adjusted the crab by one or two degrees only, and only where needle movement justified it. Drift was managed so accurately that no course regain was ever needed.
texts.marginal: SP corrected for drift within standards, but the wind correction angle was found through a series of trial headings rather than assessed, so the aircraft oscillated slowly either side of the course. The deviations stayed inside the tolerance, yet the drift is still being discovered rather than anticipated. SP is expected to assess drift from the first needle movement and to settle on a single crab angle that holds the course.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the course with the IP establishing the wind correction angle and talking through the observed drift on each leg. This is SP's first exposure to assessing drift from the needle movement, and revising the correction angle against it has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin assessing the drift independently against the needle movement, with the IP available to confirm the correction angle.
texts_at.1: SP compensated for wind to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement build to the 8 degrees limit before the crab was applied. The correction followed IP pointing out the drift rather than SP's own assessment of the observed track. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to assess the drift against the needle movement rather than relying on the briefed forecast alone.
texts_at.2: SP corrected for drift without prompting on both legs, letting the displacement re-open past 5 degrees to about 6 to 7 degrees before the crab angle was reapplied. The wind correction angle is still being removed too early, once the needle starts to return toward centre. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the established crab angle until the needle is fully centred rather than easing it early.
texts_at.3: SP established a wind correction angle appropriate to the observed drift on three of the four legs, maintaining the selected radial within 5 degrees. The fourth leg needed a small refinement of the crab after a wind shift, following the change rather than any lapse in assessment. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to refine the crab as promptly for a shifting wind as for a steady one.

texts_above.1: SP compensated for wind, holding the displacement to about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the crab angle was applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected for drift without prompting on both legs, letting the displacement re-open to about 6 to 7 degrees before the crab angle was reapplied. Holding the established crab angle until the needle is fully centred, rather than easing it early, would remove that re-opening. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid drift management.
texts_above.3: SP established a wind correction angle appropriate to the observed drift shortly after rolling out on course and maintained the selected radial within 5 degrees, refining the crab in small increments as the drift was assessed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed wind-correction technique.
texts_above.4: SP determined the required wind correction angle almost immediately after roll-out and flew it precisely, so the CDI showed no perceptible drift for the remainder of the leg, adjusting the crab by one or two degrees only where the needle movement justified it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional drift anticipation.

error_modes.label: Re-establishment of course immediately after station passage

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the course reset, the timing call and the outbound turn into the same few seconds over the station, did not re-establish the aircraft on the outbound course after station passage. The aircraft was allowed to diverge more than 8 degrees from the required radial while the cockpit tasks were still being worked. IP took control to stop the divergence and to place the aircraft on the outbound course.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the outbound course setting until after the TO-FROM indication had already changed, did not begin outbound tracking in time. The displacement reached the 8 degrees limit before any correction was applied, and the turn back toward the course was made only after IP prompted. SP recovered the outbound radial, but the sequence remained behind the aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late start of the outbound turn while the station passage indications were still being confirmed, did not roll out exactly on the required radial. The deviation opened past 5 degrees and reached approximately 7 degrees before SP corrected. SP turned back onto the outbound course promptly and stabilized on it without intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated station passage, had the outbound course set before the cone of confusion was entered and re-established tracking within 5 degrees immediately after passage. SP held the last drift-corrected heading through the ambiguity zone and resumed normal course keeping as soon as the indications settled. The transition from inbound to outbound was continuous and orderly.
texts.4: SP flew through station passage without any interruption of course keeping, holding the wind-corrected heading through the cone of confusion and resuming outbound tracking with a needle that stayed effectively centered. All cockpit tasks associated with passage were completed before the station was reached. The outbound leg began with no correction required.
texts.marginal: SP re-established the outbound course inside the tolerance, but the reset of the navigation display and the outbound turn were still being carried out at the same time, which left a short unmonitored period after passage. The result stayed within standards, yet the workload at the station is not yet spread out. SP is expected to complete the course setting before passage so that the outbound turn is the only remaining task.

texts_at.0: SP flew through station passage with the IP sequencing the course reset, the timing call and the outbound turn and talking through each step. This is SP's first exposure to the workload of station passage, and spreading the cockpit tasks across the available time has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin sequencing the passage tasks independently, with the IP available to confirm the timing.
texts_at.1: SP re-established the outbound course to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement reach the 8 degrees limit before the turn back onto course was made. The correction followed IP's prompt rather than SP's own anticipation of station passage. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to have the outbound course set before passage rather than after the TO-FROM indication has already changed.
texts_at.2: SP recognized station passage on both circuits without prompting, letting the displacement open past 5 degrees to about 7 degrees before the turn back onto the outbound course closed it. The turn is still started a moment after the passage indications are confirmed rather than anticipated before them. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate passage so the outbound turn begins as the indications settle rather than after they are re-checked.
texts_at.3: SP anticipated station passage and re-established tracking within 5 degrees immediately after passage on three of the four circuits. The remaining circuit needed a brief extra moment to confirm the cone of confusion had cleared before resuming, without a heading error resulting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that confirmation as quick on every circuit as it was on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP re-established the outbound course, holding the displacement to about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the turn back onto course was made. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized station passage on both circuits without prompting, letting the displacement open to about 7 degrees before the turn back onto the outbound course closed it. Anticipating passage so the outbound turn begins as the indications settle, rather than after they are re-checked, would remove that opening. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady handling of the passage sequence.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated station passage, had the outbound course set before the cone of confusion was entered and re-established tracking within 5 degrees immediately after passage, holding the last drift-corrected heading through the ambiguity zone. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate transition technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew through station passage without any interruption of course keeping, holding the wind-corrected heading through the cone of confusion and resuming outbound tracking with a needle that stayed effectively centered, with all cockpit tasks completed before the station was reached. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary workload sequencing.

error_modes.label: Sizing and bracketing of course corrections

texts.0: SP, due to corrections applied as large heading changes with no assessment of the resulting needle rate, did not converge on the selected course and drove the aircraft repeatedly through it. Each overshoot produced a displacement larger than the one before, exceeding 8 degrees on the opposite side of the radial. IP took the controls to stop the oscillation and to stabilize the aircraft on course.
texts.1: SP, due to a correction technique that used the same heading change regardless of how far the aircraft was from the course, did not damp the excursions either side of the selected radial. The displacement reached the 8 degrees limit on each swing and settled only after IP specified the heading to fly. SP flew the directed heading and the oscillation stopped, but not through SP's own bracketing.
texts.2: SP, due to a first correction that was not reduced as the needle began to center, did not roll out on the selected course at the first attempt. The overshoot carried the aircraft past 5 degrees on the other side, to approximately 6 degrees. SP reduced the next correction, bracketed the course and stabilized on it without any prompt.
texts.3: SP used corrections proportional to the displacement and reduced them progressively as the needle centered, staying within 5 degrees of the selected course throughout. SP bracketed the required heading in no more than two steps on each leg. The course was regained without overshoot on either side.
texts.4: SP corrected each displacement with a single, correctly sized heading change and rolled out on a heading that both centered the needle and held it. No bracketing beyond the first correction was necessary on either leg. Corrections were so measured that CDI movement stayed almost imperceptible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the course within standards, but corrections were consistently larger than the displacement required and were then taken out late, so the needle crossed center on most of them. The excursions remained inside the tolerance, yet the technique still depends on overshoot and recovery. SP is expected to size the correction to the displacement and to reduce it as the needle centers.

texts_at.0: SP flew course corrections with the IP sizing the heading change and talking through the bracketing needed on each excursion. This is SP's first exposure to proportioning a correction to the displacement, and reducing it as the needle centers has not yet become routine. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin sizing corrections independently to the displacement, with the IP available to confirm the bracketing.
texts_at.1: SP corrected course displacements to the standard expected at this stage, letting the swing reach the 8 degrees limit on each correction before the aircraft settled. The oscillation stopped only once IP specified the heading to fly rather than through SP's own bracketing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce each correction progressively as the needle centres rather than repeating the same heading change.
texts_at.2: SP bracketed every correction without prompting, letting the overshoot carry the aircraft past 5 degrees to about 6 degrees before the reduced correction closed the course. The first correction is still sized without reference to the needle rate as it approaches centre. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin reducing the correction as soon as the needle starts to move toward centre, not only after it has passed through.
texts_at.3: SP used corrections proportional to the displacement and reduced them progressively as the needle centered on three of the four legs, staying within 5 degrees of the selected course. The fourth leg needed a second small correction after an initial overshoot, without a change in the bracketing technique used. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size that first correction as accurately as on the other three legs.

texts_above.1: SP corrected course displacements, holding the swing to about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, on each correction before the aircraft settled. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP bracketed every correction without prompting, letting the overshoot carry the aircraft to about 6 degrees before the reduced correction closed the course. Reducing the correction as soon as the needle starts to move toward centre, rather than after it has passed through, would remove that overshoot. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable correction sizing.
texts_above.3: SP used corrections proportional to the displacement and reduced them progressively as the needle centered, staying within 5 degrees of the selected course throughout and bracketing the required heading in no more than two steps on each leg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good bracketing technique.
texts_above.4: SP corrected each displacement with a single, correctly sized heading change and rolled out on a heading that both centered the needle and held it, with no bracketing beyond the first correction necessary on either leg. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior correction judgment.

error_modes.label: Navaid selection, course setting and identification supporting the track

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over the navigation source selected for display and what the CDI was actually presenting, did not track the assigned course and flew to a centered needle that referred to a different selected value. The aircraft was more than 8 degrees from the assigned radial and still diverging. IP identified the incorrect selection, took control and re-established the aircraft on the assigned course.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect assumption about which navigation mode was driving the course indication, did not set the assigned course correctly before starting to track. The resulting displacement from the assigned radial reached the 8 degrees limit and was recognized only when IP questioned the selection. SP reset the source and the course and regained the radial after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed check of the navaid identification and of the selected course after the frequency change, did not begin tracking on a fully verified indication. The aircraft was allowed to drift past 5 degrees, to approximately 6 degrees, while the setup was still being confirmed. SP completed the identification, corrected back to the assigned radial and continued without intervention.
texts.3: SP selected the correct navigation source, identified the station and set the assigned course before beginning to track, then held the radial within 5 degrees. SP cross-checked the course indication against heading and bearing information at intervals during each leg. The navigation setup supported accurate tracking throughout.
texts.4: SP completed navaid selection, identification and course setting well before they were required and cross-checked the presentation against an independent bearing source. Tracking then proceeded with a needle that remained effectively centered on both legs. At no point was the displayed course accepted without verification.
texts.marginal: SP set up and identified the navaid within standards, but confirmation of the selected source and course was carried out after tracking had already started. Course keeping stayed inside the tolerance, yet the verification remains reactive. SP is expected to complete selection, identification and course setting before turning to track, and to state the active mode as part of the setup.

texts_at.0: SP set up the navigation source with the IP confirming the selection, the identification and the course setting before tracking began. This is SP's first exposure to verifying which navigation mode is driving the course indication, and confirming it before tracking has not yet become a fixed habit. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin verifying the navigation source independently before tracking, with the IP available to confirm the selection.
texts_at.1: SP set up the navigation source to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement reach the 8 degrees limit before the correct source and course were confirmed. The reset followed IP questioning the selection rather than SP's own check of the indication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to verify which navigation mode is driving the display before setting the course from it.
texts_at.2: SP verified the navigation setup without prompting on most legs, letting the aircraft drift past 5 degrees to about 6 degrees once before the identification was completed and the course corrected. That check is still made after tracking has already started on the leg where the frequency had just been changed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete identification before tracking begins on every leg, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP selected the correct navigation source, identified the station and set the assigned course before beginning to track on three of the four legs, holding the radial within 5 degrees. The fourth leg needed a brief cross-check against heading and bearing information before the setup was confirmed, without a deviation resulting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to complete that cross-check as promptly on every leg as on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP set up the navigation source, holding the displacement to about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the correct source and course were confirmed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP verified the navigation setup without prompting on most legs, letting the aircraft drift to about 6 degrees once before the identification was completed and the course corrected. Completing identification before tracking begins on every leg, rather than most of them, would remove that drift. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured navaid-setup discipline.
texts_above.3: SP selected the correct navigation source, identified the station and set the assigned course before beginning to track, then held the radial within 5 degrees while cross-checking the course indication against heading and bearing information at intervals. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise setup verification.
texts_above.4: SP completed navaid selection, identification and course setting well before they were required and cross-checked the presentation against an independent bearing source, with tracking proceeding on a needle that remained effectively centered on both legs. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate navigation discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to attention devoted entirely to the course display while a correction was being flown, did not maintain the assigned altitude during tracking and allowed a descent to develop with the aircraft out of trim. The altitude error exceeded 300 feet and continued to increase without being recognized. IP took control to recover the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to an altimeter left out of the cross-check while the drift was being assessed, did not hold the assigned altitude on the outbound leg. The deviation reached the 300 feet limit and remained there until IP called the altitude. SP then returned to the assigned level, but only after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to bank inputs made without the small pitch compensation they require, did not hold the assigned altitude during the corrections back to course. The deviation passed 150 feet and reached approximately 250 feet before SP noticed the trend. SP corrected pitch and power in good time and regained the assigned altitude unaided.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the inbound and outbound tracking, including during the turns onto correction headings. SP kept the aircraft trimmed so that heading changes did not disturb the pitch attitude. Altitude control remained steady while the course work was being carried out.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitude with deviations that were negligible for the whole exercise, with the aircraft trimmed and the altimeter effectively static. Corrections to course produced no change in the vertical profile. Altitude required no comment at any stage of the tracking.
texts.marginal: SP held the assigned altitude within standards, but the altitude was maintained by repeated small pitch corrections rather than by a trimmed attitude, with a consistent tendency to lose height whenever a course correction was flown. The deviations stayed inside the tolerance, yet the coupling between the turns and the pitch is not yet controlled. SP is expected to trim the aircraft properly and to add the small pitch compensation as bank is applied.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the course with the IP calling the altitude trend and talking through the pitch compensation needed as corrections were flown. This is SP's first exposure to holding altitude through correction turns, and adding pitch compensation together with the bank has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin adding the pitch compensation independently as the bank is applied, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held altitude to the standard expected at this stage while tracking, letting the deviation reach the 300 feet limit before returning to the assigned level. The correction followed IP's call rather than SP's own cross-check of the altimeter through the correction turns. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the scan through each turn onto a correction heading rather than only after it.
texts_at.2: SP maintained altitude without prompting through the corrections back to course, letting the deviation pass 150 feet to about 250 feet before the trend was noticed and corrected. Pitch is still compensated for bank a moment after the bank input rather than together with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add the small pitch compensation as the bank goes in rather than after the altitude has already begun to move.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the inbound and outbound tracking, including during the turns onto correction headings, on three of the four legs. The fourth leg showed a brief excursion during a busy frequency change without any change in the trim technique used. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same altitude discipline through a busy setup as through a straightforward one.

texts_above.1: SP held altitude while tracking, containing the deviation to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, before returning to the assigned level. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP maintained altitude without prompting through the corrections back to course, letting the deviation pass 150 feet to about 250 feet before the trend was corrected. Adding the pitch compensation together with the bank input, rather than a moment after it, would keep that excursion smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the inbound and outbound tracking, including during the turns onto correction headings, keeping the aircraft trimmed so heading changes did not disturb the pitch attitude. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed trim technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitude with deviations that were negligible for the whole exercise, with the aircraft trimmed and the altimeter effectively static, so corrections to course produced no change in the vertical profile. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior altitude-and-trim coordination.

error_modes.label: Airspeed and power control while maintaining course

texts.0: SP, due to a power setting carried over from the previous exercise and never checked against the indicator, did not maintain the briefed tracking airspeed. The speed departed the briefed value by more than 20 knots while SP remained focused on the course indication. IP directed the power correction to restore the briefed airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete cross-check in which the airspeed indicator was not scanned during the correction turns, did not detect the speed trend building on the inbound leg. The deviation reached the 20 knots limit and stayed there until IP called for a power adjustment. SP reset the power, but the correction was made only after the verbal prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a power change made for the turn and not reset on roll-out, did not hold the briefed tracking airspeed. The deviation passed 10 knots and reached approximately 15 knots before SP recognized it. SP restored the required power setting promptly and stabilized the airspeed without intervention.
texts.3: SP set and held the briefed power for the tracking exercise and maintained the airspeed within 10 knots on both legs. SP made small power adjustments where the turns or the altitude corrections required them and returned to the known setting afterwards. Airspeed remained stable throughout the course work.
texts.4: SP established the briefed tracking airspeed at the start of the exercise and held it with deviations that were barely perceptible. Power was moved only where the profile genuinely required it, and always in a single measured adjustment. Airspeed control did not compete with course keeping at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the tracking airspeed within standards, but the speed was corrected in large power steps that produced repeated small excursions either side of the briefed value. The result stayed inside the tolerance, yet the power required for the condition is not yet known by feel. SP is expected to set a known power value and to correct in smaller increments so that airspeed settles without repeated overshoot.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the course with the IP calling the airspeed trend and talking through the power settings needed for the turns and corrections. This is SP's first exposure to managing power through correction turns, and returning it to a known setting on roll-out has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin resetting power independently on roll-out, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held airspeed to the standard expected at this stage while tracking, letting the deviation reach the 20 knots limit before the power was reset. The correction followed IP's call rather than SP's own cross-check of the airspeed indicator during the correction turns. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to include the airspeed indicator in the scan through every correction turn, not only after a deviation is called.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed airspeed without prompting on most corrections, letting the deviation pass 10 knots to about 15 knots once before the power was reset. Power set for a turn is still left unreset on roll-out on that leg rather than returned to the known setting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to return power to the known setting on roll-out every time, not only most of the time.
texts_at.3: SP set and held the briefed power for the tracking exercise and maintained airspeed within 10 knots on three of the four legs. The fourth leg needed a small additional adjustment following an altitude correction, without affecting the standard held. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep airspeed as steady through an altitude correction as through a course correction.

texts_above.1: SP held airspeed while tracking, containing the deviation to about 20 knots, at the tolerance limit, before the power was reset. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the briefed airspeed without prompting on most corrections, letting the deviation pass 10 knots to about 15 knots once before the power was reset. Returning power to the known setting on every roll-out, not only most of them, would remove that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent power management.
texts_above.3: SP set and held the briefed power for the tracking exercise and maintained the airspeed within 10 knots on both legs, making small power adjustments where the turns or the altitude corrections required them and returning to the known setting afterwards. error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check integrating course display and flight instruments

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the course indicator, did not monitor the aircraft state during the tracking legs and did not detect the developing course and attitude errors. The course displacement passed 8 degrees while bank and assigned altitude were also allowed to change unnoticed. IP took the controls to restore both the aircraft state and the course.
texts.1: SP, due to an absent cross-check of aircraft state against the primary flight instruments, did not correlate the CDI indication with heading and attitude and applied corrections that the actual aircraft state did not support. The course displacement reached the 8 degrees limit before the error was recognized following IP's comment. SP re-established a working scan and regained the course only after that prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that dwelt too long on the navigation display after each correction, did not keep the scan rate needed to hold the course and the flight parameters together. The course deviation opened past 5 degrees and reached approximately 6 degrees before it was seen. SP resumed a regular cross-check, corrected back to the radial and continued unassisted.

texts.4: SP maintained an even and continuous cross-check in which the course display was one element among the flight instruments and never the focus. error_modes.label: Inbound re-intercept angle kept below 90 degrees (course arrow above the 90 degree index)

texts.0: SP, due to a re-intercept flown with the course arrow below the 90 degree index, that is an inbound intercept angle of 90 degrees or more, did not convert the displacement into a controlled closure back onto the radial. The closure rate was far higher than the turn could absorb, the CDI swept through center and the aircraft ended up more than 8 degrees off the selected course on the opposite side, still turning away. IP took the controls, reduced the angle to the course and re-established the aircraft on the radial.

texts.2: SP, due to an intercept angle chosen larger than the displacement justified when the needle began to move off center, did not roll out on the radial at the first attempt. texts.3: SP re-intercepted the course with the head of the course arrow kept in the top half of the instrument case and every intercept angle comfortably below 90 degrees. The angle was scaled to the deflection so that the needle closed at a workable rate, and the displacement never exceeded 5 degrees. Both the inbound and the outbound legs were regained without swinging through the radial.
texts.4: SP built each inbound intercept heading from the course arrow to the bearing pointer plus 30 degrees construction and never allowed the arrow to approach the 90 degree index. texts.marginal: SP regained the course inside the tolerance, but the intercept angles were habitually taken close to the 90 degree index even for small deflections, so the needle arrived at center much faster than the roll-out could handle. error_modes.label: Turning in the shorter direction toward the CDI when regaining the course

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started the longer way round instead of turning in the shorter direction toward the CDI, did not begin closing on the radial and increased the displacement for the whole of the turn. texts.4: SP took the shorter way to the needle immediately on each occasion, with the turn direction established before the bank was applied. error_modes.label: TO indication checked after the inbound course is set (avoiding reverse sensing while tracking)

The tracking was accurate, yet the sense of the display is being confirmed by the behaviour of the aircraft rather than by the indicator. texts_at.0: SP set the inbound course with the IP calling for the TO indication check and confirming the sense before the first correction was flown. The displacement from the course stayed within 5 degrees throughout. The roll-out reference was applied consistently on both legs.

error_modes.label: Heading bug marked with the intercept and wind-corrected heading as a tracking reference

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the heading bug where it had been set for a previous leg instead of marking the intercept heading with it, did not have any heading reference for the course being flown and steered back to the old bug. The aircraft was taken onto a heading unrelated to the radial and the displacement grew beyond 8 degrees with the error unrecognized. IP took the controls, re-marked the required heading and re-established the aircraft on the course.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting to mark the intercept heading with the heading bug, did not hold a stable reference after the roll-out and allowed the heading to wander several degrees off the wind-corrected value. The resulting displacement built to the 8 degrees limit and was addressed only after IP asked what heading was being flown. SP set the bug and returned to the radial after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading bug left on the raw course value rather than on the wind-corrected heading actually required, did not fly a reference that held the aircraft on the radial. The deviation opened past 5 degrees and reached approximately 6 degrees on the downwind side. SP moved the bug onto the corrected heading, regained the course and held it without intervention.
texts.3: SP marked the intercept heading with the heading bug before each turn and moved it onto the wind-corrected heading once the drift had been assessed. Heading was then held against the bug and the deviation from the radial stayed within 5 degrees. The reference was updated at every course change.
texts.4: SP set the heading bug on the intercept heading before starting each turn and re-marked it on the drift-corrected heading immediately after roll-out. Heading was flown against that reference so closely that the CDI showed no perceptible movement and deviations remained negligible. The bug reflected the required heading at every stage of both legs.
texts.marginal: SP kept the course within standards, but the heading bug was updated after the aircraft had already been established rather than before the turn, so for short periods the bug indicated a heading no longer being flown. Course keeping remained inside the tolerance, yet the reference lags the aircraft. SP is expected to mark the intercept heading with the bug before the turn and to move it onto the wind-corrected heading as soon as it is established.
